summary:
Marswalk · Gale Crater  is an integrated task-management and dual-interface navigation ecosystem engineered to guide NASA astronauts safely during Martian Extravehicular Activities (EVAs). This platform (tablet application) bridges the communication and data gap between Base Control and field explorers.

The system workflow begins with a centralized Admin Dashboard, where mission commanders can seamlessly assign specific exploration tasks, track progress, and oversee the safety of the crew in real-time.

To maximize astronauts' situational awareness and operational efficiency, the field system is split into a unique dual-device architecture:
1. The AR Head-Up Display (HUD): A primary visual interface that keeps the astronaut's "eyes up." It projects critical, glanceable survival data—such as remaining oxygen, current time, and Augmented Reality (AR) directional arrows—directly onto the physical environment.
2. The Tactical Handheld Device: A secondary, detailed terminal for deep environmental analysis. It provides the astronaut with dynamic 3D route information, real-time radiation levels, humidity metrics, hazard alerts, and communication logs.

By separating critical survival navigation from complex environmental data, and connecting it all to a streamlined Admin assignment system, Marswalk · Gale Crater empowers future explorers to navigate hazardous Martian terrain confidently, complete tasks efficiently, and return to base safely.
details:
On Mars, one wrong route can end a mission. Marswalk is a mission-planning tool for walks on Mars. Mission Control plans a safe route from NASA data and prepares the crew; the astronaut follows it with a tablet and a heads-up display (HUD) controlled by hand gestures.

Try it yourself: marswalk.atly.my

On the sign-in page, under "Try Marswalk", tap Mission Control or Astronaut. No passcode needed. For the full experience, use two devices: Mission Control on one, the astronaut on the other.

Prefer to type a login? Use these test accounts:

  1. Mission Control · ID: MW-CREW-0008 · Password: 12345678
  2. Astronaut · ID: MW-CREW-0007 · Password: 12345678

Suggested path:

  1. As Mission Control, plan a route and send it to the astronaut.
  2. As the Astronaut, open the mission and tap Start journey.
  3. Watch the walk live on Mission Control's Live page.

Each screen opens a short tutorial the first time; the ? button replays it.

1. The problem

Planning a trip on Earth is easy: a map app finds the route, and help is close if something goes wrong. A walk on Mars is different. Planners must weigh steep slopes, rocks, loose sand, radiation, solar storms, limited oxygen and the scientific goals, for the way out and the way back. A call for help takes up to about 22 minutes to reach Earth, and the first crewed Mars mission has been estimated at around $500 billion (a figure cited in a NASA technical report, 2020). A planning mistake can waste the mission or endanger the crew. Marswalk brings these factors together before anyone leaves base.

2. Who is it for?

Mission planners and Mission Control, who plan and watch the walk; scientists, who choose what to study; and astronauts, who carry it out.

3. What it gives them

  • Routes built around the science: pick a target such as clay minerals or rock chemistry, and Marswalk suggests stops on safe ground and the safest route there and back.
  • Risks caught before departure: slopes, rocky ground, loose sand, the oxygen margin, radiation, seasonal temperatures and solar storms forecast for the planned date.
  • A crew that is ready: a pre-departure checklist of what to bring for the tasks and for safety, based on the route and its risks.
  • Support during the walk: hands-free guidance on the HUD, detail on the tablet, and live oversight and emergency tools for Mission Control.

4. How it works

① Plan the mission (Mission Control)

  • Form the team (Commander, Crew Geologist, Health & Safety Officer…), choose one of six areas along NASA Curiosity's path in Gale Crater, and set the departure date.
  • Choose what to investigate; Marswalk places checkpoints on safe ground and finds the safest route there and back on the USGS 1 m terrain model. Each checkpoint shows its ground (e.g. "Safe ground, 2°").
  • Customise everything: add or drag checkpoints, and give each astronaut tasks, picked from a list for their role or written by hand.
  • Check and send: the Caution list shows every risk on the route, with this route's numbers. Mission Control confirms the risks before sending.

② Prepare the astronauts

  • The departure date is checked against NASA's solar storm model (DONKI). A storm predicted within 2 days of departure raises a caution. If departure is further ahead than any forecast exists, Marswalk says "no forecast yet" rather than "safe".
  • Marswalk suggests a checklist, split into "To do the tasks" (camera, sample bags…) and "To stay safe" (suit check, radio check, dosimeter…), with the reason for each item. Mission Control can remove or add items; the astronaut ticks them off on the tablet before starting.

③ Carry out the walk (Tablet + HUD)

  • Tablet: a mission dashboard with the astronaut's tasks at each checkpoint, Mission Control's note, the team, the rules and Curiosity's own photos of the sites ahead. On the walk: NASA science layers, photo pins previewing what the astronaut will see, checkpoint photos, messages, Hold to talk, I'm OK and Need help. One tap on Abort plans the safest way home.
    • Thumbs-up → sends "I'm OK" to Mission Control.
    • Open hand, then fist → takes a checkpoint photo.
    • Hand wave → asks for help; the tablet asks the astronaut to confirm, then the call goes to Mission Control and the team.

④ Monitor and respond (Mission Control)

  • The Live page shows each astronaut's position, oxygen, status calls and a body cam (a still picture from their HUD camera, about once a second). Mission Control approves checkpoint photos, plays voice clips, sends messages and can end an astronaut's walk.
  • Rescue route: when an astronaut calls for help, every teammate's tablet plans the safest route to them at once, and their HUD shows the distance and direction.
  • History keeps every walked path, photo and task.

NASA data and where we use it

  • HiRISE colour mosaic, 25 cm (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter): the ground on every map.
  • Gale terrain model, 1 m (USGS Astrogeology, from HiRISE stereo images): the safest route, the rescue route, the ground rating at each checkpoint, the steep and rocky cautions, and the HUD's warning signs.
  • CRISM mineral maps (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter): clay, water-bearing mineral and olivine/pyroxene layers, used to pick and suggest stops.
  • THEMIS night-time infrared (Mars Odyssey): tells loose sand from bedrock, for those stops, the loose-sand caution and the HUD's sand signs.
  • Curiosity's path and waypoints (NASA MMGIS): the rover's real path and the key sites you can tap. Missions start on the side facing Curiosity's landing site, Bradbury Landing.
  • APXS rock and soil chemistry (Curiosity; Canadian Space Agency instrument; NASA PDS): the chemistry layer and the rock chemistry, soil and sulfate stops.
  • REMS weather (Curiosity; Centro de Astrobiología, Spain): outside temperature, pressure and UV on the tablet, and typical temperatures for the season of the departure date, from past Mars years. Not a forecast.
  • RAD radiation dose (Curiosity): the radiation caution and reading. A Gale average, not a live value.
  • Navcam and Mastcam raw images (Curiosity, NASA raw image API): the rover's photos of key sites, on the dashboard and as photo pins on the walk map.
  • DONKI solar storm model, WSA-ENLIL (NASA CCMC, api.nasa.gov): solar storm cautions for the departure date. A model estimate, not an official forecast.
  • NASA Mars Trek: linked from planning and the dashboard for a 3D view of Gale Crater.
  • Curiosity's proposed path up Mount Sharp: linked from planning to show where the rover heads next.
  • Perseverance raw images: linked from the walk screen's navigation info. NASA's Mars Global Localization matched Perseverance's camera panoramas to orbital images; Marswalk's position fixes follow that idea and are simulated.

How we used AI

  • Coding: we built Marswalk with Claude Code (Anthropic). The team set the goals and design, tested every feature on our own devices and decided what to keep; Claude wrote much of the code and the data-processing scripts.
  • Gesture recognition in the app: Google's open-source MediaPipe gesture model runs on the HUD phone to recognise the hand signs.
  • Video: the teaser's voice-over is an open-source AI voice (Kokoro); editing was done with Claude Code and ffmpeg. All screen footage is the real app, and the hand-gesture shots were filmed by the team.
  • Images: ChatGPT helped design the video cover; the HUD photo and logos on it are real.
  • Writing: AI helped draft and edit this description; the team reviewed it.

Built with TypeScript, React, MapLibre, Cloudflare and Python/GDAL. This is a prototype: suit readings, position fixes and the demo walk are simulated, some tablet readings are sample values, and the hand gestures were tested with bare hands, not EVA gloves.
